That this House condemn the government for its lack of a sincere commitment to the environment and for its vacuous discussion paper which completely fails to offer the concrete action that all Canadians would like to see implemented and, therefore, call on the government to end the rhetoric and to introduce a truly substantial environmental action plan.
She said: Mr. Speaker, as you know, we as members of the opposition tend to make political speeches and indulge in political rhetoric from time to time. However, when the Minister of the Environment was appointed by the Prime Minister, we had high hopes that he would be able to further the cause of the environment within the Conservative Party.
In 1984, the Prime Minister claimed to be concerned about the environment, but between 1984 and 1988, he started slashing funding-as much as 95 per cent in the budget for alternative resources.

We had a lot of hope for the Minister of the Environment when he was chosen by the Prime Minister. He was supposed to be a great friend of the Prime Minister. He was supposed to be close to the Prime Minister. He was supposed to be the minister who could put environmental action on the map in so far as this government is concerned.
In actual fact what we have seen is not only a first term chequered by environmental cuts, hatchet jobs and axes
but we have seen a year and a half in the second term of a majority Conservative government in which the new Minister of the Environment has done nothing more than talk about what he might do for environmental change.
He started off with a 200-page document which actually had some teeth.

This particular document mentioned some real solutions for dealing with PCBs and proposed a new energy consumption policy for Canada. Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Minister of the Environment is trying to cut back on garbage, because today, what we have is a mere 30 pages that are more or less garbage, don't mean a thing, and demonstrate that we Canadians are the most wasteful country in the world and the country that consumes the most energy. Whether we are talking about electricity, water or any source of energy at all, Mr. Speaker, Canada is one of the most wasteful countries in the world, and I think it all starts here in the House. We know that words are wasted, because we just saw a member who was afraid to speak himself because he didn't want his own comments and environmental issues to be on the record. He is ashamed of his government's record on PCBs.
He is ashamed of his government's record on PCBs. He is ashamed of his government's record on oil spills, particularly oil spills off Vancouver Island.
I am sorry if his government has made Canada the dumping point of American refrigerators. You can walk through any-

-dump in the province of Quebec and you will see refrigerators full of CFCs in Canadian dumps, because the Government of Canada thinks it is good business to bring garbage from the United States to Canada.

Shame!

Not only are we the Americans' dumping ground when it comes to our foreign policy, but now we are literally their garbage can.
What we expected from the environment minister, Mr. Speaker-and I know that it is very hard for the hon. member to face facts, because the hon. member for Abitibi is really caught now; the GST has 17 per cent support in the polls and 17 per cent is very low. I know it is hard when you have an "environmentalist" government.
I remember very well, Mr. Speaker-the Prime Minister himself said so last week and again yesterday in the House-I was shocked to hear him say that he had created the policy to clean up Hamilton Harbour.
Mr. Speaker, I had something to say about that, because as you recall, Mr. Speaker, the Hamilton Harbour issue dragged on for three years. The Prime Minister did not want to do anything. It took a by-election to get something done. It would be good if we could have by-elections in all ridings every year-then we might have an environmental policy. But we cannot wait for the government to make little promises during election campaigns.
For example, Mr. Speaker-

Listen to this if you want a chuckle, Mr. Speaker. Thank God it is printed on recycled paper because it is going to be used for many other things.
Canadians need to explore the ways governments, industry and
individuals can best contribute to a 50-per-cent reduction in waste.
Do you know what they want to do to reduce waste in government? They want to open an office of waste management so that they can put out more paper.
They are actually talking about opening an office of waste management to examine ways of how we can cut down on our waste.
In this document national regulations to control packaging and to require recycling are an option. On an issue as important as over-packaging, which is something that every consumer understands and every consumer is revolting against, why do they not introduce national regulations on the controlling of packaging and then let the public have a discussion?

We are not against a public debate, Mr. Speaker. Since 1984, the Conservatives have been promising a debate on it, but they do not have the courage to take a position on such an important issue as packaging.

The issue of the controlling of packaging is only one of the elements that has been raised in this document. Once again, they talk about, for example, the greenhouse effect. They ask themselves whether or not we should be developing on a national basis greenhouse gas emission targets.
We do not have time to ask ourselves that question. Of course we must establish greenhouse gas emission targets. We must set them in regulation so that Canadians can then have some input into what level they might be set at. But this document is nothing but a stall tactic.

I can see very clearly that the government will hold public hearings across Canada from now until June, while the debate goes on. But what will it do next fall? It will bring in an environmental policy that will take effect after the next federal election.
But the people of Canada believed the Prime Minister when he went to Burlington-

When the Prime Minister came within breathing space of my riding-he did not dare go into my riding-he actually went to the Canada Centre for Inland Waters and said that he was the environment Prime Minister for Canada. He promised that he would bring forward a green policy that would make Canada proud in the international arena for having a real green policy. Instead, what he has dropped with this document is a green bomb which does not give a single substantive piece of action on issues like greenhouse gases, global warming, old growth forests, national parks, water or energy.
This government does not have the guts to come forward with a single substantive policy because all it wants to do is talk out the clock. It would be amusing to watch the government talk out the clock if it were not for the fact that the global clock is ticking.
March 30, 1990

Friends of the Earth, along with a number of environmental groups across the country, put forward a document called "The Green Print for Canada". It has some teeth in it, although it is not a perfect document. There are some additions, omissions and addenda, but it is the basis for real environmental discussion, which should have been the basis for the document tabled by the Minister of the Environment.
I am not surprised that the Minister of the Environment was afraid to come into the House to defend his policy. It is an embarrassment. It is a recycled bunch of old promises that could verily be characterized as a green bomb for the Minister of the Environment and the Prime Minister.

You remember, Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister appointed the environment minister, we talked about "mini-bouche" and "maxi-bouche". We know that "maxi-bouche" changed places and became transport minister-You know, Mr. Speaker, this document actually talks about a transport policy at the same time as the government cut VIA Rail!

They cut VIA Rail only a few months ago. Now they have the audacity to suggest that we should have a national transportation policy that reflects a clean environment. If anybody had seen the environmental assessment that was allegedly an addendum to the VIA Rail analysis, one could see quite clearly that they went ahead with the VIA cuts with absolutely no consideration for the environmental impact.
If any Canadian has had the displeasure recently of motoring between Windsor and Montreal in the so-called corridor area, they will know that with the increased traffic in the Toronto-Niagara belt alone we are choking in our own carbon dioxide fumes. We do not need more talk. We do not more questions. We need some specific emission reductions. We need some specific targets.
This document should not be a document asking questions. It should be a document providing answers.

Hear, hear!

It is not too much to ask. I am sure that all of those on the other side of the House who believe in a green Canada would realize that if we truly endorse the concept of sustainable development, if we truly recognize the meaning of Brundtland, then we must believe that the federal government must have the power of environmental review in every major megaproject of the nature of the Rafferty-Alameda. It seems to me that in the Rafferty-Alameda dossier we have a very good example of how the Minister of the Environment talks a very good game when it comes to the environment but is unprepared to act.
I think it is a tragedy that in the Rafferty-Alameda decision it was not the Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada that protected the rights of the people to a full and fair environmental assessment, it was the courts. Now the Minister of the Environment is coming in with a proposal to water down the provisions of the law that require the federal government to undergo a full environmental assessment. He is parading
that under the guise of strengthening the law, when in actual fact the two successive decisions of the court have shown that the law provides the protection. It is the government that is not prepared to act when it comes to truly carrying out the responsibilities it was given under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act is one way of ensuring that Canadians' rights to a clean environment are protected. But we need to go a step further.
Absent from this discussion paper-this vacuous discussion paper-is the capacity of Canadians to sue the government. I think we have to examine the possibility of class action legislation which will permit any Canadian to be granted intervenor status. When the air we breathe is poisoned and when the water we drink is full of toxins to the point that in the latest report of the International Joint Commission for the first time a direct link between neurological damage in human beings and the poison in the water we drink has been discovered, then we have the right and a responsibility as a society to make sure that every Canadian can pursue the government with the full intent of the law when the government fails to respect its own laws.
We recreate in the forests that absorb the greenhouse gases. Every time a tree is felled it does not touch one person, it touches all Canadians. We have a right and a responsibility as a society to make sure that every Canadian can pursue the government with the full intent of the law.
I can understand why this Conservative government would not want to move with an environmental auditor, in the same way as the Auditor General has shown himself to be independent of government.

I think that if we had an auditor general for the environment, like the auditor general we have for financial matters, we would have something specific that would give Canadians an opportunity to complain about the departments without dealing directly with the government.

We need some very specific legislative changes to reduce waste, not only in the disposing of waste or in finding ways of dealing with the toxins that we create but also to reduce waste at the input level. We need to develop solutions to the crisis that makes Canadians the

We are sitting in a green chamber. Is it not about time that the good will and the forward thinking that was demonstrated by the Speaker of the House be translated into action in all federal government departments?
We are not only talking about regulations that must be brought forward to deal with garbage and waste at the private sector level and at the community level. We must lead by example. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate on behalf of my colleague, the hon. Minister of the Environment, who is absent today keeping a long-standing commitment to make a speech to the Inter-American Development Bank. We all know that is something very important because the issue we are discussing today has many international dimensions.
I want to start by welcoming the hon. member for Hamilton East back to the green chamber. I appreciate very much her plea for a non-partisan, rational, compassionate approach to the issue. I want to welcome her back with all her enthusiasm and partisan venom. She stated that she has been travelling in areas where environmental situations have caused neurological damage. It should suit her very well to be a leadership candidate, if that is the approach the Liberals will introduce to this critical debate.
That was the International Joint Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
She wants goodwill. Her speech hardly had any phrases that would bear any relationship to goodwill. The Liberals had been in power for 25 years and, if we are truly in such a mess, how can they stand up today and blame it all on other people?
Yesterday, on behalf of the Government of Canada, my colleague, the Minister of the Environment, invited all Canadians to participate in the reshaping of our future. Judging from the speech we have just heard from the hon. member for Hamilton East, there is a clear indication that more Canadians have to get involved in the debate if we want this debate to have any substance.
I am pleased to speak on behalf of the minister today. The goal of the federal government is quite clear, and that is to make Canada by the year 2000 the world's most environmentally friendly country. That would be in keeping with the image that we still enjoy throughout the world. It is not one we have particularly earned, but one
that we inherited because of the vastness of our land and the pristine mountains, waters, streams and forests.
Let us take a look at what is proposed. The next steps are equally clear. The Green Plan is a national challenge, a framework for achieving this goal. It has four parts.
The first step is to inform Canadians about the challenges we are facing and the imperatives that must be addressed. Between mid-April and mid-May there will be information sessions in 30 cities across the country. We are hoping to engage every Canadian in every part of our country.
The second phase involves seeking the views of Canadians on specific issues raised in the framework for this discussion paper. This phase will last from May 21 to the end of June. We will be asking Canadians in groups or as individuals to make their submissions to us.
The third phase will involve the final formulation of the action plan which will be tabled in the House of Commons this fall.
Finally the plan will find implementation.
A clear goal, a clear timetable and a clear commitment to action, the plan is designed to position the federal government in a leadership role, to bridge the gap between those who have old fashioned views about development and those who say that all development must stop, that we must reach back to the dark ages and even beyond that where all of us could afford to live in a hunting and gathering economy.
This issue crosses political lines. It requires the co-operation of all Canadians. It requires us to put aside our partisan views about these issues and to engage ourselves in this dialogue.
All of us on this side of the House share the desire of Canadians, indeed the impatience that Canadians feel for action, but as the framework for discussion paper makes clear, the achievement of sustainable development requires more than the series of react and cure actions by government. If sustainable development is to become a reality we need a blueprint for lasting and long-term change.
We must also realize that going it alone as Canadians is not the solution. We are just now learning how inextricably our resources, the life sustaining systems, and the ecological zones and regions over which we claim sovereignty ourselves are interrelated with all the ecological zones of the planet; how Canadians will be affected by the destruction of the rain forests in the
March 30, 1990

Amazon; and how other people on the planet could be affected if we do not improve our custodial practices over our own resources.
At the turn of the century there were 1.5 billion people on the planet. By the end of this century there will be 6 billion people, and that figure will perhaps double by the year 2020. What a daunting challenge: all these people will lay claim to some of the scarce resources, the scarcity in what the planet can produce for its human species.
Everywhere we look we see the symptoms of a planet under stress: the thinning of the ozone layer, the threat of climate change, environmental emergencies, and the disappearance of plant and wildlife species. They make us wonder about our relationship with our environment and the future we are creating for our children. They make us raise fundamental questions about whether the living standards that we have worked so hard to achieve can really be maintained.
As Canadians we are blessed in both material and environmental terms. Much of our material well-being has its basis in our endowment of renewable and non-renewable resources. More than four million Canadians, one in every three working Canadians, are employed in our five main resource based industries: agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining and energy. We are a product of the environment, a participant in its evolution, and a significant factor in its present character.
Canadians are the heaviest users of energy per capita in the world. In the process of burning fossil fuels, Canadians are the world's fourth largest producers of carbon dioxide on a per capita basis. The average Canadians produces almost two kilograms of solid waste per day, more than any other citizen of the world, and less than 10 per cent is recycled. A Canadian family of five produces, on average, more than 2,000 litres of waste water every day.
Canadian governments, business and individuals have not been indifferent to environmental issues. Over the past decade there has been a strong and a steady record of achievement in the environmental field, despite what the hon. member for Hamilton East says, yet the

symptoms of environmental degradation continue to multiply.
Clearly we have to change some of our most deeply ingrained assumptions and habits if we are to live up to our responsibilities as stewards of a large portion of the world's environment and continue to enjoy the quality of life to which we have become accustomed. Perhaps we have to liberate ourselves from that part of our North American culture in which only big is beautiful: big cars, big homes, big plants, big mills and factories, big corporations and big cities.
In the area of Canada from where I come, most people do a day's work by the time people in the large cities get to work, spending up to one and a half to two hours a day smelling the exhaust fumes from the automobiles in front of them. Can we really sustain this kind of senseless development?
We already know that it will cost billions of dollars- and no one has found a source for the money-to rebuild the municipal infrastructures, the sewers that discharge into our rivers, our lakes and our oceans. Can we really sustain that kind of culture, that kind of habit, that kind of lifestyle? It means nothing less than the restructuring of our everyday lives and our families and our homes from the time we get up in the morning until we retire at night.
I do not anticipate it to be much different in Canada, but I have a chart which shows the annual release of dioxins in the United States by various sectors.
In the United States municipal solid waste incineration makes up 60.3 per cent of all dioxins discharged into the atmosphere; fuel combustion, 15.4 per cent; secondary copper furnaces, 11.2 per cent; forest fires, 4.5 per cent, and I would think that it is a much higher percentage in Canada; publicly owned treatment works, 2.6 per cent; magnesium production, 2.4 per cent; hospital waste incineration, 1.4 per cent; and pulp and paper mills, 0.8 per cent. Of course multinational corporations operating pulp mills are easy targets for the environmentalist. The truth is that all of us as individuals in our collective activities, in our cumulative human activities in the large cities, are perhaps the biggest polluters. That is the nature of the environmental challenge we face.

We cannot afford the costs of environmental degradation and mismanagement, nor can we afford the costly react and cure approach to dealing with environmental problems.
The government firmly believes that sustainable development can only be achieved through fundamental changes in the way we make decisions at all levels, including our personal lives as individuals managing households and choosing lifestyles, as working people making choices about production processes, energy uses, waste disposal and packaging, and as elected officials setting the rules for economic activities and environmental management in pursuing our international agenda.
This government understands that environmental problems are the result of the failure of all of us to make decisions that fully take their environmental consequences into account. It is the countless day to day choices we make that shape our economy. In turn, the flow of energy, materials and waste set in motion by these decisions determine the impact of our actions on the natural environment and ultimately on our own well-being.
This is not wilful irresponsibility. Choices are often made without adequate knowledge or understanding of the ways in which we interact with the environment every day, but sustainable development requires that our decisions reflect the true value of our scarce environmental resources and the fragile ecosystems on which we depend for our health and well-being.
It is not good enough to point fingers every time a new discovery is made, every time we learn to measure in even more minute quantities. Back in the 1930s and 1940s we measured in parts per thousand or parts per million. Of course anything that was not detectable was safe as far as the environment was concerned. Then we began to measure in parts per billion and parts per trillion. Today we can measure in parts per quadrillion, and we can trace harmful agents through to living organisms. We do not yet understand the health effects in total, but nevertheless every time a new discovery is made a finger is pointed at someone asking why it has not been corrected.
There is more to it than that. Improved decision making is at the heart of the government's long-term strategy for sustainable development. Improved data,
improved information, improved science will be the basis of this decision-making process.
We need to forge and strengthen new partnerships. We all share the environment, and we need to work together to preserve and to protect it. Co-operative efforts are essential at the international level and domestically. We need to co-operate with the provinces that share and have most of the regulatory and legal powers to make some of the changes and the corrections that need to be made.
Of course action is also required to address immediate environmental problems related to the health concerns of Canadians, and action has been taken. In the House the Prime Minister gave us a very impressive list of some of the things that have been done over the last five years in the Great Lakes, in dealing with our air quality and with acid rain, and even in cleaning up the Hamilton harbour.
The government believes that action on environmental problems should be targeted at five broad areas: the key stresses on the environment and human health associated with toxic substances, waste and environmental emergencies; our shared environmental resources, air and water, including issues such as global warming, ozone depletion, acid rain, toxic air pollutants and local air and water quality; managing our renewable resources of agriculture, forests and fisheries on a sustainable basis. This is perhaps our biggest challenge because we are so dependent on these prime resources for our economic well-being. We are aware now, all of a sudden, that we cannot decouple the economy from the environment, one in every three Canadians being directly or indirectly involved with these resource industries.
The fourth target is preserving and protecting Canada's unique ecological heritage resources, parks and wildlife. We are now learning that in Canada we have roughly 39 ecological zones, and they do not neatly fit within the artificial political boundaries within which the federal and provincial governments exercise jurisdiction. Here again there needs to be federal-provincial co-operation. In every one of the ecological zones we need to set aside areas that are critically important in protecting their natural features.
March 30, 1990

Canadians and indeed all citizens of the world are at a critical stage in the evolution toward sustainable development. The Government of Canada believes that sustainable development offers the promise of a lasting solution to environmental problems. To bring about sustainable development, Canadians and their governments must proceed to develop an action plan that removes obstacles for better decision making. The government is prepared to bring forward a comprehensive national framework for implementing sustainable development.
If The Green Plan is to succeed, however, it will require the commitment of Canadians both individually and collectively. It will require us to participate in an over-all global effort to make sure that other countries are making the same decisions. If Canadians are to be called upon to make that commitment and to pay the cost, then they have a right to expect to be involved in defining the problem and developing the solutions. This is why we have chosen this course of action. That is why the government and I urge all Canadians, including all the members of the opposition, to join us in this necessary exercise of consultation.
The Green Plan is this government's strategy for the environment. It is a strategy with a clear goal, a clear timetable and a clear commitment to action. We invite all Canadians to participate in the national challenge of reshaping our future for ourselves, for our children and for all future generations.

I look now to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, as to whether or not you will hear me for a few moments while I make the case, not to reiterate, I might add, what was raised in the House the other day but on a new point of order.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member of the New Democratic Party appears to be referring to citation 821 of Beauchesne's sixth edition which reads:
(1)	All rulings of the Chairman may be appealed to the committee.
(2)	There is no appeal to the House from the Chairman's ruling except by way of a report from the committee.
If the committee were to report to the House in respect of some matter; in other words, if the committee were to ask the House for a ruling, then it would be appropriate for the House to rule.
To suggest that in fact we could now go back and somehow annul the decision taken by the committee chairman, approved by the committee under a vote, because the general subject matter of the committee, namely the bill, is now back in the House is to distort the meaning of citation 821, very clearly.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I want the hon. member to know that I appreciate what the government House leader and the hon. member for Kamloops are saying.
He cannot re-argue what he has argued before. I would like him to state whether there are new arguments and, if so, I will give him the opportunity to present them.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me make it perfectly clear that I am not asking that what was done in the committee be somehow undone today. As I indicated, I am not suggesting a repeat of the previous day's arguments.
I have a single point of order I wish to make. I want to take a few moments to make it because I believe this is a most important matter. I would suggest that the chair of a committee has no authority to invoke closure in that
committee the way it was done in this instance. What is being used by the chair of the committee as a precedent ought not to be accepted as a such. That is the point I want to make in some detail with the Chair at this point. I do not want to take up much time, because I recognize it is an opposition day and I want to keep my comments very brief.
As I said, I consider this matter to be one of the most important procedural questions that we will have to consider, including yourself, Mr. Speaker, in our term of office.
As I indicated, the chairman of the finance committee mentioned last week that Speaker Brandt raised this issue 100 years ago. Whether Speaker Brandt's solution was a service or a disservice to parliamentary democracy is a very debatable point. What is not debatable is that it changed forever the balance in the House of Commons. If the solution of the hon. member for Mississauga South as chairman of the committee becomes precedent, there is little doubt that it will leave as profound and long lasting a change to the equilibrium of this House as did Brandt's decision in Westminster.
For this reason, I think it is imperative for the House to reflect carefully on the proceedings of this committee and I hope you, Sir, will permit me a few moments to express our concerns.
I do not think we can in any way consider the proceedings in the finance committee last week to be merely a series of events and decisions, as you, Mr. Speaker, described the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs back in June 1984. I must say, like it or not, a precedent is now being set.
First,the chairman of the finance committee used the Lachance incident as a precedent. It was repeatedly referred to as such in the finance committee, even after the Speaker's caution last Monday that "neither this House nor the Speaker gave the incidents any value whatsoever in procedural terms."
The point is that the chairman of the finance committee on numerous occasions, as I sat in on that committee proceeding, repeated time after time that this was the precedent he was quoting: the Lachance decision back in the justice committee in 1984. If this incident is now used as a precedent, what then will two such incidents become? They will obviously become tradition and con-
March 30, 1990

vention that will be used by chairs of committees from now on.
Because I do not think the attempted birth of a closure procedure in committee can at this time be reviewed as an isolated incident, I want to say that as a minority party in this Parliament we can only see it in concert with what has been to us an alarming increase in the use of closure and time allocation and a severe diminution of the ability of minority voices to be heard.
Six years have passed between the Lachance ruling and the ruling of the hon. member for Mississauga South, just as six years used to pass between one closure in this House and the next. In today's parliamentary environment we can expect that this tactic, if it is allowed to become a precedent, will be used again, again and again.
The question I would like to address is whether or not you as Speaker and the House have an obligation to review what transpired in the finance committee during the review of Bill C-62, the act to implement the goods and services tax.
You, Mr. Speaker, and previous Speakers have repeatedly decided that "matters and procedural issues that arise in committees ought to be settled in committee unless the committee reports them first to the House". It has been quoted time and time again by yourself and other Speakers.
There are countless precedents where complaints and grievances arising from committees have been brought to the attention of the Chair, and the decision of the Chair has remained always to remain disengaged from whatever the dispute may be.
Nonetheless, Mr. Speaker, I think there are important distinctions between this particular incidence and many of the precedents and compelling reasons for the Chair and the House to reflect and decide upon this particular case.
You have rarely been asked, Mr. Speaker, to rule on the actions of committee chairmen which were as serious or as irregular as those which we saw in the finance committee last week.
Routine Proceedings
The unfortunate ruling by the chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in 1984 was one occasion.
Another was a case in 1919 when the House considered the second report of the "Special Committee appointed for the purpose of an inquiry forthwith as to the prices charged throughout Canada for foodstuffs, clothing, fuel and other necessities of life".
When concurrence was moved in that report in 1919 an hon. member raised his concerns about voting irregularities in the committee. Specifically, he was concerned that while he had the utmost confidence in the chair and did not mean to do anything which would denigrate the reputation of the chairperson, he pointed out that the chairman actually voted twice. He voted during the proceedings and again once to break a tie.
The member argued that "the report which purports to be the report of the committee on the cost of living is not the report of the committee, and that it should be sent back for further consideration". I am quoting from his comments in Hansard.
In other words, the member argued that the process was flawed, and that the committee should be told to go back and do it again.
On that occasion the Speaker in the chair did not buy that argument and permitted the House to concur in the committee report. Because that 1919 incident has like the 1974 incident become cited as precedent, I would like to point to an important distinction between the situations that faced the Speaker of that day and what faces us today.
On that occasion back on July 1, 1919, the Speaker ruled, and I quote:
The House is only seized of the proceedings of the committee from the report that it gets from the committee. There is no reference in the report whatever to any question having been raised in committee and therefore my ruling is that it is not competent for this House to go back of the report which is in its possession now.
The difference is that today this House is seized of the proceedings of the finance committee. They have just been tabled. There is reference in those proceedings to the question having been raised in the committee.

March 30, 1990
Routine Proceedings
Therefore I submit that it is appropriate for the House to "go back of the report which is now in its possession".
Those in your chair, Mr. Speaker, have usually maintained that they can only deal with committee issues when a report is made to the House or when a report on a given issue is made to the House. I suggest that that has now happened. The chairman of the finance committee has through one of its members presented to the House not only Bill C-62, in its amended form, but also the minutes of the committee meetings in which the bill was studied. The House now has in its possession, referred to it, if you like, all the evidence presented to the committee, as well as a detailed report of how the committee's decisions were made.
Included in the evidence attached to the report is the ruling made by the chairman on Tuesday, March 20, which has been the focus of so much concern. Also included are the minutes which show that this ruling was sustained when it was challenged and the minutes which show that a motion of censure was put in the committee but never decided upon.
This motion of censure was debated for several hours. No member of the committee attempted to amend it or soften it in any way. The meeting was adjourned by a committee member before the question was put, and the committee decided to adjourn without having made a decision whether or not to censure the chair.
Where does this leave the House? The committee has failed to report formally on the chairman's unusual actions, either endorsing them or censuring them. The committee has failed utterly to reach a decision on whether or not the actions of the member for Mississauga South should be censured. We all recognize the importance of a decision being made on his actions, particularly the controversial ruling of March 20.
The committee may not have made a decision, but the House in some manner must now.
If you accept the argument, Mr. Speaker, that a decision must be made at this point either to ratify the process by which this committee arrived at its report and make it a precedent or nullify it to preserve the rules as they were applied up until last week, then I would like to make a few closing remarks on just how that decision could be made.
Some months ago, when ruling on a question of privilege raised by the former Leader of the Official Opposition, the Speaker referred to a difficulty familiar to those on this side of the House. Chiefly, if the government has made a mistake, even inadvertently, if a motion is put to the floor of the House which reflects poorly on the government, that motion will invariably be voted in the negative.
For example, Mr. Speaker, if I could have convinced you to accept a prima facie case of privilege had been established and you had permitted me to move a motion of censure in this House on the activities of the committee or the chair of that committee, you and I both know that that motion would have been defeated. And the precedent would have been firmly established that committee chairs when faced with circumstances they do not know how to handle can resort to unilateral and arbitrary rulings.
That is why most procedural points are not decided by the majority. Either the rules are followed as governed by the Chair or the House decides unanimously to suspend the rules. The majority has the right to govern and the right to control the House but reasonable limits are placed on those rights. Some things cannot be done by a simple majority as they were done in the committee. They must be done unanimously.
I think that this issue as to whether or not a committee chair can invoke closure cannot be decided by a majority of one committee late one night after a marathon sitting. Nor can it be decided fairly by this House when such a decision would be clouded by the circumstances surrounding it, a highly controversial money bill, a mistaken sense of it being a confidence issue, and an extreme sort of atmosphere of hostility between the parties.
Members of the House and, I would submit, Mr. Speaker, all parliamentarians maintain that the House is by tradition and law a court, a very high court. We claim the right to oversee our own procedures and internal operations and take considerable measures to resist any infringement of our authority.
However, I am not convinced that we should maintain that authority-and I am sure many of those who elected us might agree-if we do not exercise our powers and authorities responsibly. If we are court, then we should act like a court. If we are masters of our own procedures
March 30,1990

and rules, then we must ensure that these are mastered, not mutilated.
I am not a lawyer but I hope others here who are will at the appropriate time tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in our justice system a natural justice is always enforced. If a process is followed in our courts that is seriously flawed and demonstrated to be unfair to one side, then the result of that process is appealable to a higher court.
I think of the recent examples Canadians have witnessed when the courts turned to the government and said: "The way you conducted your environmental assessment was flawed. You did not follow the rules. You did not play fair. Go back and do it again properly".
Similarly, if in a court of law witnesses are prevented from being heard or evidence is withheld in a manner which is not consistent with legal traditions and precedents, then the outcome of that proceeding is appealable. In the justice system a mandatory instruction can in fact be issued. A decision can in fact be overturned.
I suppose the question is: Is a lesser standard of justice then applied in this House? Will a lesser test be put in the process to decide to impose a tax on virtually every good and service than was applied to the process to decide on dams and pulp mills?
I am asking for your guidance, Mr. Speaker, on the following questions: Has a precedent been set by the chairman of the finance committee in his ruling of March 20, 1990? Does a committee chairman have the right to impose closure or time allocation without debate or without decision by the committee? Has the review of the finance committee of Bill C-62 been tainted by the chairman's March 20 ruling? Last, if it has been tainted, is the report of the committee still receivable by this House?
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I am also going to make a request. Your panel of chairs for legislative committees has been developing a code of conduct. In this House we notice that the chairs are voluntarily restraining themselves from even voting at second reading on bills and are taking other steps to ensure that they not only act impartially but are seen to act impartially. It would be most helpful, Mr. Speaker, to all members of this House if this protocol could be more formally codified, printed
Routine Proceedings
and distributed to all offices, to enhance all of our understanding of the role of chairs when legislation has been referred to committees. I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, your willingness to hear me out.

Mr. Speaker, one of the components that I wish to add to the evidence that my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops, has presented, I do not think is a component that should be decided this afternoon. That component is that in the very committee that the member has raised these questions about, the chairman of the committee moved a motion himself in the middle of debate.

We would then have the precedent that in any committee, at any time, the chairperson could just move a substantive motion, not one to adjourn or not even to ask for a motion, but just move a motion and that is it.
I do not think that we want to rush into a quick answer on this. I understand the government's need for urgency. I understand the agenda. I am not suggesting that the majority need be compromised by that urgency, as they see it. The danger and the argument that invalidates the minister's reference to Beauchesne's is that we are here at the time of report on the precipice of establishing a principle that could be referred to by succeeding Parliaments that would hamper important decisions being made properly.
Routine Proceedings
To quickly move into a decision that would encompass an experience that we have had, that may or may not have been intentional, of a chairperson actually moving a motion that would become an integral part of the business could mean that the Chair itself could use that reference in the House someday and the Chair's authority could be extended to absolute rule.
I was profoundly moved by the detailed presentation by my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops. I was very, very interested in seeing the support from the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and the Liberal House leader. I think this kind of decision, albeit we have important matters in front of us, is the very foundation on which eastern European countries are examining parliamentary democracy.
These kinds of small, separate things begin to build up as precedents and erode and evaporate the power of the total House are matters of grave concern. A 48 hour delay to allow intelligent, thoughtful analysis, not only by the opposition, but by the government, is absolutely essential.
Some day the Tories may be in opposition again, and we do not want a repeat of Tories running down the centre of this Chamber yelling at the Chair with rule books in their hands because a motion overtook their reason and logic because the rule was not clear.
I am not suggesting that anybody would be as irresponsible on this side of the House and behave the way that group did at that time. But if we allow this kind of precedent to be established, then that benchmark of terrible behaviour as evidenced by the Tories could be emulated. We want to save the House from that kind of behaviour happening ever again. No one should behave like the Tories did at that time, ever again.
Mr. Speaker, I urge you, we need the 48 hour delay. We need caution, prudence, wisdom and thoughtfulness before we allow this to slip into a precedent and allow ourselves to be bound by that precedent.

Mr. Speaker, I speak as a member of the finance committee which was engaged in the study of this bill.
The points that I want to put in front of you, in addition to those which my House leader has so ably explained, are points which refer to the effects within committee of the ruling which was placed to control committee activity by the chair of the committee. It was a ruling which, certainly in our view, made it extremely difficult for there to be valid and full consideration of Bill C-62 to be given within the committee, as was required when it was referred to it by this House.
The points that I want to refer to are four in number. The first is to buttress the point which my House leader has put forward.
It should be quite clearly seen by you, Mr. Speaker, and by the House that after the statements referred to by which the chair imposed a certain order of procedure, which he thereafter referred to as the Lachance rule, the Speaker in his ruling on the matter this week made it quite clear that there was no precedent to be attached to what took place in the 1984 committee. In fact in his ruling he made it absolutely evident that one should attach, as he put it, any "procedural flags" to what should only be regarded as an incident which had occurred within a committee.
Despite this, there was continual reference by the chair of the committee throughout the period of consideration of the bill to this as a precedent and, indeed, to the Speaker's ruling as a ruling which supported him as chair of the committee in determining that it was a precedent.
He also pointed out, and I say this simply for purposes of your information, Mr. Speaker, that he had been told of the Lachance incident by the clerk of the committee and that it was on that basis that he moved forward. Despite the fact that the Speaker quite clearly indicated to the House that the affair in 1984 should be considered simply an incident, it was clearly taken as a precedent by the chair of the committee and consequently imposed throughout the remainder of the considerations.
Routine Proceedings
The second point which I want to make is that as a consequence of this order-and here we come to some of the rights of members of the House being undercut by what took place-a motion was moved by one of the Conservative members of the committee, Mr. Couture, to amend Bill C-62. That amendment was not permitted to be put before the committee, despite the fact that there was considerable interest in it on the part of a number of members of the committee representing all three parties.
Thus the consequence of the ruling has been to prevent a specific amendment from going forward to the floor of that committee despite the interest of all three parties in the amendment itself.
The third point I want to make to the Speaker is that as a consequence of the way in which the order was set out by the chair of this committee, it was not possible for the clerks of the committee and the clerks' branch to put in front of us as members of the committee prior to the start of clause by clause consideration of the bill the set of amendments which had been presented by all members of the committee to the committee clerk.
I raised this question in committee and the clerk was not able to give me a satisfactory explanation. Despite my request and that of other members that the amendments should be in front of us on Monday at the start of clause by clause consideration, the clerk was not able to give me any explanation as to why these amendments were not in front of us except on the day of the actual consideration of the group of clauses to which the amendments themselves referred.
Mr. Speaker, you can recognize that with the incredible complexity of the goods and services tax bill to have simply received at the last minute these amendments and to have to peruse them virtually as they were moved was not a satisfactory and acceptable way for members of this House to seriously perform their duties as members of Parliament and as members of the committee.
I could expand on that point, Mr. Speaker, but in view of the time I will not.
The fourth point that I want to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, is this. It has become clear in further detailed perusal of the 1984 decision of Mr. Lachance, which the member for Mississauga South claimed as a precedent for his actions as the chair of that committee,

March 30, 1990
Routine Proceedings
that it was not in fact followed in the case of the actions of the hon. member for Mississauga South. I refer specifically to something which bothered me particularly. As my colleague for Edmonton East indicated in the discussion of this matter last week, one of the particular points which comes to be important is whether a chairperson of the committee can take action when that action is something which is already covered by the rules set down in our Standing Orders.
In the case of the particular action taken by the member for Mississauga South, his action was to deem withdrawn the motion which was on the floor of the committee. That, as the member for Edmonton East indicated, is something that is covered in the Standing Orders. For such a withdrawal of a motion to take place, unanimous consent is required. The member for Mississauga South claimed that the preceding incident as I will refer to it and as the Speaker referred to it, was, in fact, a precedent which permitted him, as chairman, to deem such a motion withdrawn. In fact, in further detailed checking the so-called Lachance incident in 1984, we find that no such action was taken by chairperson Lachance. Chairperson Lachance instead suspended the motion which was in front of the committee, and then announced his ruling with respect to the further points of importance to the committee's further activities. At that point, he put forward his intention to resign. What we find, Mr. Speaker, with further perusal of Mr. Lachance's decision is that the decision was not followed by the member for Mississauga South with respect to his procedures within this committee.
Therefore, we have without doubt a clear precedent, a clear breaking of the ice made by the chair of this committee, something which he claimed in committee when, following the suggestions of the Speaker, we raised these questions on Monday in committee and the chair of the finance committee claimed that it was Mr. Lachance who had broken the ice.
In fact, the chairman of the finance committee himself had taken a procedure with respect to deeming a motion withdrawn, something which is quite clearly set out in the rules that we have to follow in this House and in
committee. He took that position without any previous incident or event to which he could refer.
All of these questions have been raised in committee, so this is not the first time they have been raised. Having raised them in committee, I feel I must raise them here now because the only protection for the minority and ultimately for the majority is that the democratic rules which are set down for Parliament must be followed. They cannot be picked and chosen on the part of committee chairmen or the Speaker of the House. They are rules which govern us all. That is what the rule of law is about in my view and, as a member of the finance committee, that is why I feel that this is such a crucial issue to bring before the House of Commons itself.

The principle of the common law, Mr. Speaker, is quite clear, and that is that there is a requirement for natural justice, and this committee has been bulldozed by its chairman, who used bully tactics on the opposition. From the evidence we have heard, if you can call it evidence, but certainly from the witnesses who were there, on his own volition he chucked out some motion that was currently being debated before the committee, without seeking the consent of the committee, and the committee was seized with the motion.
Your Honour knows perfectly well that once this House is seized with a motion it cannot be withdrawn by the mover without the consent of the House; it has become, in some sense, the property of the House. I understand in this committee the motion that was the property of the committee and was being debated in the committee was withdrawn by the chairman, unilaterally.
That is highly improper and contrary to all of the traditions of this House. As the previous speaker on behalf of the Liberal Party put it, there are number of things that happened in that standing committee of which members of the House are just becoming aware. We all know about the ruling that insisted that the committee in six hours would review clauses 13 to 66 of the bill and then vote on them and any amendments. We all know that the Chair in his order, in his ruling, a ruling that was not asked for by any member of the committee, ruled that the debate must finish by Thursday afternoon and that the committee must report today. We all know that he said that opposition parties would be allowed one minute per amendment and that other members of the committee would be allowed one minute per amendment.
I just discovered this morning that the Chair did not enforce that rule when he did not wish to enforce that rule. I would submit that since the committee itself has not dealt with the privilege motion, the motion to have the member removed from the chair, that there are many things we have to worry about with regard to the conduct of the Chair, with regard to whether or not this report is admissible, whether or not the House can feel any confidence that we followed the process set out in the standing orders to have a report stage which is preceded by clause-by-clause study in a committee.

I would ask and request that the Speaker make sure that all members of this House and members of that committee have a full opportunity on Monday to explain their grievances against the Chair and against the committee and to explain why they believe that the committee report on the goods and services tax is inadmissible to this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take overly long to intervene on this point of order because certainly this is an opposition day, the day provided for the Official Opposition. It is unfortunate that the NDP has decided to take up so much of that time but I think we as government members must respond to this point of order.
I have heard a lot of talk here this afternoon indicating that we are dealing here with fundamental principles. I agree with that. We are dealing with fundamental principles, but the fundamental principle that is being forgotten in this process, and the one that I think has been very clearly abused by the NDP members is this: There is a fundamental principle that the opposition has a right to oppose but the government must, in the end, have the right to govern. It must be able to proceed with its legislation.
That is the very fundamental and probably the most important principle of a parliamentary democracy. I think that is the question that we really are looking at
Routine Proceedings
here today. It is not what happened with the chairman's ruling in the committee. It is why the chairman had to rule as he did. Because, Mr. Speaker, if we look at the point of order that has been raised before us today, I think, first of all, there are a few things that have to be said.
First, as you have said several times, the Speaker has already ruled on the substantive part of this issue. The Speaker has clearly said that he does not accept this as a precedent of any longstanding. It is not a precedent with which this House is seized. I understand that argument and I am not prepared to argue that.
But the NDP members continue to insist that even after the Speaker has ruled, and even after that process was completed in the finance committee, somehow they should once again be allowed to derail and throw off the tracks this whole process. Of course, that is what this whole thing is really about. It is really a way of the minority once again acting in a tyrannical fashion or to use their own words, "putting the jackboots to Parliament". That is essentially the kind of activity that we are seeing.
You know, Sir, as Speaker, that one of the very important, fundamental roles of the Speaker is the obligation to maintain order. Of course that same principle applies to the chairman of a committee. The chairman must try through whatever means he or she has to maintain order in the committee.
What we were dealing with here in this particular committee was not your run of the mill committee behaviour. In fact, what you are dealing with, Mr. Speaker, was very extreme behaviour by the NDP party. Extreme to the point that I am not sure any of us, certainly in my memory, in my 10 years here in the House, have I seen that kind of behaviour of people running around with little pink pillows, slippers on their feet and bells on their toes! I mean, Mr. Speaker, surely, if ever there was an example of extreme childish behaviour, that certainly was the case.
Now, if my memory serves me, the committee had sat in a marathon sitting for something like 36 hours. Thirty-six hours of non-stop sitting simply because the NDP members were not prepared to deal with substantive debate to allow the House and committee to proceed. They wanted strictly to play games, not only as they had demonstrated in this committee, but as they

March 30, 1990
Routine Proceedings
had demonstrated previously here in this House. That is what we have been living with now for several weeks, to the point that the third party have themselves so pumped up that they now think they are the Official Opposition. They now think they have the right to tie up the House of Commons, to tie up the committees, to do whatever they choose and totally frustrate the government from its right to govern. And I might add, Mr. Speaker, the right of the Official Opposition to perform their role. We see by the very fact that the NDP members have raised this point of order today that this is a demonstration of their arrogance and their callousness.
We have an issue which we consider important. It is an issue on the environment which has been raised by the Official Opposition. But what has happened? The NDP member chose to raise a point of order. They have now used up almost one hour and a half of time that could have been used to debate that issue. They chose to do that, I argue, not because of what happened in the finance committee but because they have chosen to demonstrate to this House that they are going to derail, threaten, intimidate and do whatever they have to do to delay this House, the government and even the Official Opposition from performing their roles.
Let us return to that basic fundamental principle of a government being able to govern, and a chairman being asked to maintain order. One of the things that I think we have to remember is that we were dealing with a very extreme circumstance. The behaviour of the chairman of the committee was not something that is done every day.
Why was it done this time? Because the circumstances in which the committee found itself was a circumstance that was in itself extreme. It required an unusual approach by the chairman. The chairman had to take some very unusual approaches in order to maintain order and decorum in that committee. The chairman had to keep order. The point we are making is that order had to be maintained with extreme actions.
One other point I want to make is that we have a very fine balance of rules in this House to protect the rights of the majority and to protect the rights of the minority. We had in this committee a demonstration of those rules working. What happened is the chairman took a very
unusual action to solve a very unusual problem caused by the childish behaviour of the NDP. What followed is what should happen. Immediately there was a challenge to the chairman's ruling. The question was put to the committee and the committee sustained the chairman. The rules were being followed in exactly the way that they should. There was the check and the balance that was necessary to make sure that the chairman did not in any way abuse his or her authority.
Not only have we got a ruling in the House on this particular issue, we also have a decision of the committee sustaining the role of the chairman and the action of the chairman because the chairman was dealing with extreme childish behaviour on the part of that third party, which was disrupting all of the rights and opportunities of both the government members and the Official Opposition members.

Routine Proceedings
It has been a longstanding practice, going back to the beginning of the parliamentary system, that Speakers from time to time make rulings that are not covered in any kind of exact way by the Orders of the Day. The House then can divide on whether or not to uphold the Speaker. That is what happened in committee. It is not the first time it has happened in committee. I suggest to you it will not be the last time. The minority cannot be allowed to hijack the business of the people, to cause extra expense for the people, and on and on and on.
We have dealt, in this Chamber, with the provision of two rules that have to deal with the issue before us today. We have had for many years a closure rule that is put without debate or amendment, and the House divides. That could have been done. We have another form of limiting debate called time allocation. Members will know that this Chamber decided that the maximum length of time for debate on time allocation is two hours in the Chamber.
That party, with its pillows, blankets and bells on their toes debated a time allocation motion for better than 31 hours, 15 times the allowable time in this Chamber, at great cost to the taxpayers of this nation.

The reason I am saying that is that 16 years ago the other government, the Liberal government, said essentially the same thing: that we need to be consulted before action is taken. It is a bit much, after 16 years, to have a Conservative government, two years after being re-elected on an environmental platform, coming out with the same need for consultation. Many people expected the government to put the accent on action. A number of consumer groups and environmental groups have criticized the government, and I respect the hon. minister's response that there were a number of groups which have supported the government's lack of action. There are also a number of groups, such as Friends of the Earth, which say that there is no action at the moment but just a way to delay action in the future.
There are people who expected action from this government. The people from Saint-Basile-le-Grand expected action from this government. I have a letter here from the mayor of Saint-Basile-le-Grand who is still waiting to see the government show leadership on the treatment of PCBs. There are two resolutions from the city of Saint-Basile-le-Grand, asking the government to act. Unfortunately, the document that has been given to us in The Green Plan has nothing that would
benefit the people of Saint-Basile. It has nothing that will benefit the people of Saint-Amable, where there are problems with mounds of tires.
I know that whenever we are uncomfortable with the response on the government side, we can say that it is provincial responsibility, but even then we are coming into a serious situation because the province is not accepting this. I can tell you that even in dealing with James Bay, Phase II, the government is faced with a serious problem and that it cannot even get its act together with the provincial Government of Quebec as to how to hold hearings.

Mr. Speaker, I may add that I was very disappointed in the Green Plan released by the Minister of the Environment yesterday. I have known the minister for a long time, and I know him as a man of integrity, and a very competent man, who is not being used to best advantage by this government. I am sure he was very disappointed to see the action plan's initial 250 pages-whose contents were no secret-reduced to 30 pages with four pages of notes, two in French and two in English. I think it is unfortunate to see an Environment minister reduced to endorsing lack of action on the part of the federal government.
All I can say is, we have no answers to the questions the government wishes to raise-because basically, the document contains only questions-we have only questions. These questions have been asked before, and I have the paper here. They were asked during a CROP poll, and I am referring to the one in May 1988, which is a good example.

I would like to bring to the attention of the House and particularly to my hon. colleague, the Minister of Forestry, that the questions he is asking in this Green Paper have already been asked two years ago, and the answers were very surprising.
For example, the willingness to pay is a very major question: the willingness of Canadians to pay. What is it? Well according to this survey, a national survey, 8 out of 10 Canadians are willing to pay extra for environmental
March 30, 1990

protection. How can my hon. colleague, the Minister of Forestry, say that that question has not been answered? It has been answered. In fact it seems that Canadians across the country are more in favour of paying for controlling pollution than polluters themselves or even the government. It is not the time to re-ask the question.
But I just want to bring to the minister's attention several points here about willingness to pay. Not only 8 out of 10 Canadians, approximately 78 per cent, said they were willing to pay extra for increased spending on environmental protection, but when Canadians were asked to choose between alternative mechanisms for this contribution, almost one in two, almost 50 per cent, said they would be willing to accept a 1 per cent surcharge on their income taxes. Canadians are willing to pay extra to clean up the environment. Is the government doing its part? Not by re-asking the question it is not.
In addition, Canadians have expressed themselves very clearly about toxic chemicals, another question which is asked in the minister's Green Paper, and is being asked again after two years. In the survey that was done two years ago, toxic chemical pollution came out as being at the very top of the list of environmental concerns, along with clean water supply. It even surpassed acid rain as an issue in 1988, and only one-third of Canadians believed that the mechanisms now in place to control toxic chemicals are adequate to ensure public safety. Over two-thirds of Canadians feel that in the toxic chemical area the government is not doing its job.
Environmental health is one question that concerns most Canadians. The concern about environmental health is one to which Canadians responded most emphatically, and that is another question being re-asked two years later. Asked about how concerned they were about environmental pollution, eight out of ten Canadians again said they are very concerned about human health and safety. Their second major concern is for future generations. Further questions on possible impacts of pollution reveal that nine out of ten Canadians believe that many peoples' health has already been affected by existing pollution levels. That means that they feel that the cancer that is going to be caused, and the people who are going to be affected have already
Supply
become affected. What a sad thought, that we are already at the point of no return. No wonder that this is one of the major concerns of Canadians because of the health aspects.
With respect to the role of government, and this is what I would like to put the emphasis on, Canadians want government to get tougher with polluting industries, not as this paper seems to indicate and to enforce the law. In a poll two years ago, Canadians said obviously we want you to get tough. We want you to apply the law to polluting industries. Seven in ten Canadians currently believe that governments usually side with the industries that pollute rather than siding with the affected public.
Let us look at this. Over two-thirds of our citizens believe that the government is on the side of the polluters. Does that have any relationship to the Conservatives' low standing in the polls? The government does not have the confidence of the people on the question of the role of government and pollution control.
I would just like to close here by saying that I think the government had a choice. It could have done better. I have tried to raise the point that because of its corporate donations, its corporate ties, it has a tendency to side with polluters. Everybody knows it. Rather than coming out with actions, it comes out with recycled rhetoric. It is unfortunate. I suppose the only way that that problem can be addressed is through the ballot box. Therefore I would just like to present my opinion that the government has a chance. It has another chance. It has three years perhaps left in government. It can do a better job. The people of Quebec and the people of Canada are expecting the government to do a good job. It is awfully unfortunate that our friend and colleague, the Minister of the Environment, would be so badly used by this government and abused when he was brought into this government to do a good job.
In conclusion I would like to I move:
That the House continue to sit beyond the ordinary hour of daily
adjournment for the purpose of considering the motion standing in
the name of the member for Hamilton East.
