Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by quoting from Hansard. I hope these words sound familiar to the members of the government. I think they should re-read them.
The ozone layer above that protects the earth from the sun's ultra-violet rays is diminishing. TWenty-two billion tonnes of carbon dioxide from fossil fuels are being pumped into the world's atmosphere each year. This C02 is heating up our climate, with hazards we are only beginning to understand. Moreover, forests which process carbon dioxide are disappearing at a breathtaking rate: Tventy-five million tons of sulphur dioxide fall every year in Canada and the United States in the form of acid rain that is destroying our lakes and rivers, damaging our forests and monuments, and threatening our health.
It is well past the time that these issues be not only addressed but resolved.
Those are the words of the Prime Minister as reported in Hansard for April 6, 1989.
What do we have as a result of all that deep understanding of the seriousness, the urgency and the immediacy of the problem and the need for action now? What we have nearly a year later is still no environmental protection legislation or environmental assessment legislation. There is still no action plan on the environment. We have instead cuts to environmental programs and cuts in budgets.
It is a great pleasure today to rise and expose this green plan for the sham it is, for the contradiction it presents to every action of the government since it took office in 1984.
This green plan is a litany of broken promises. That is what it is. It is going back five years. It is contradicting everything the government has said it is going to do. It is full of words like "could consider", "might consider", "could consider proposing", "should we", "could we". It is too late for all that. The Prime Minister knew that a year ago. He said it clearly. Yet what has he done about it?
Yesterday, we had a litany of the supposed accomplishments of this government on the environment. I want to go through a litany of failures-not only of failures, which implies lack of action, but actions damaging to the environment.
The Green Plan talks about the preservation of wildlife. Yet the government cut $3.8 million from the budget of the Canadian Wildlife Service.
We have lots of discussion about parks and expanding our national parks system. This is the government which weeks ago voted against a motion to expand the parks system to make a real firm commitment to parks consistent with our international commitments.
The report talks about shipping and disposal. Can I remind the government that it was five years ago that the spill of PCBs at Kenora occurred, and that for three years following that nothing more was heard about PCBs except promises of action? There was no action taken until weeks before the 1988 national election when suddenly disaster hit Saint-Basile-le-Grand and PCBs were again a problem and suddenly they were on the public agenda. This time it was right before an election and there was some interim action.
March 30, 1990

But do we have a comprehensive plan for handling the disposal and transportation of PCBs? No, we do not- five years after the spill at Kenora.
There is talk in this report about toxic substances and protecting the health of Canadians. This is the same government that is now saying that the Centre for Occupational Health and Safety should become a selfsupporting income-generating institution and that in fact it should not be available to Canadian workers to give them information on toxic substances and other health hazards in their workplaces.
This report talks about research. Yet we have seen virtually the decimation of research at the National Research Council. In fact, we have seen the breaking down of that institution that has been fundamental to the progress of science, research and technology in this country for decades.
The government appears not to be aware that in fact Canada's environmental work-indeed the space program-started with atmospheric research by the National Research Council in the mid-thirties when we started looking at what was happening in the Arctic and began studying the aurora borealis. Now, about 55 years later, this government is systematically dismantling the National Research Council. How dare it publish a document like this and talk about improving science and research?
The document talks a lot about information and the importance of it. This is the very government that suppressed a major report on toxic substances called "Storm Warning". It suppressed it for over a year, keeping it from the people of Canada.
This government talks about better environmental assessment. I have heard comments in Question Period today and yesterday, as well as the debate today, about the weakness of the current legislation and the current environmental assessment process. If it is weak, it is weak because the government and its ministers refuse to meet their legal obligations under that legislation. Those legal obligations have been spelled out by the courts, not once but three times. It is about to happen again. Once again, the government is not fulfilling its responsibilities for the environment, responsibilities it has been reminded of three times by the Federal Court. Instead, it is leaving it to voluntary organizations with their own
Supply
resources and on their own initiative to do what the government is legally obligated to do.
It is over two weeks since the decision of the court on the Oldman River dam which said, first, the federal permit allowing that construction was cancelled; and, second, that two ministers of the Crown were obliged to conduct environmental assessments. The government has done nothing. It is still considering the implications of the decision.
I will tell you the implications of the decision. It is this simple. A multi-million dollar project in Alberta with severe environmental impacts has gone ahead for an additional two and one-half weeks and this government has done nothing about the fact that it is proceeding absolutely illegally without a permit that it is required to have under the Navigable Waters Act.
If the government was serious it would look at that decision on the Oldman River dam. It would say what the courts have clearly said, that it has not only the right but the responsibility to carry out an environmental assessment on every project that touches an area of federal responsibility. It would be environmentally assessing James Bay, II, if it would stop fooling around with discussions that are going nowhere with the province of Quebec and get on with its responsibility and its job. It would be environmentally assessing Point Aconi. It would be looking at its options for the Carmanah Valley.
Actions speak louder than words. Thirty pages of words do not say much against four years of not only inaction but negative action against the environment.
The plan purports to deal with the question of CO2 emissions. Members of the government may not be aware of this, but the environment committee of the House has been looking intensively at global warming. There is one clear message-and it is not new-the single, most efficient, most effective, most cost effective thing we can do to stop global warming is to cut the emissions of CO2.
Action on that front is clear. By conservation alone, we could cut 52 per cent of CO2 emissions. This government has known now for five years what needs to be done. It is not doing it.
Instead, it has cut wind energy research at the National Research Council. It has cut the environmental secretariat at the National Research Council. It has, over-all, cut money spent on alternative energy and

March 30, 1990
Supply
conservation-the single most effective thing that we can do to save this planet-from $500 million to a miserly $50 million.
The Minister of Finance can get up and talk about the financial reserves all he wants. That is window-dressing. There are no financial reserves. The reserves in this year's budget, as he knows perfectly well, have but cut and not increased to accommodate the environment or anything else.
The Green Plan talks about biological diversity. Just this past week, 10 people at the National Research Council, including five senior research officers in the biological section, were laid off.
We have broken promises. We have had repeated promises over the last year, and I am sure before I entered this House, to table environmental assessment legislation. We have repeated promises that we will have a strong action plan by this spring. March 21 was over a week ago. That was the beginning of spring, and this is all we have.
It is also important to talk about what is not here. What is not here is any strong commitment by the government itself to act on its own, to ensure that all governmental practices are in accordance with the principles of sustainable development. What minister has said to his department: "Before you produce your budget, I want to know everything you are doing that has an impact on the environment. Where it is a negative impact, I want you to change it. I want to know how we are using the world's resources. Where it is excessive I want you to change it. I will not approve a budget until I have those answers." Not one minister has said that to his or her department. That is the way this government needs to operate.
We have the Minister of the Environment saying: "Environment is the responsibility of every minister". Then we have the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology saying instead: "The environment is nice. It is like poetry and flowers, kind of fun to have but it has nothing to do with the economy".
This is the government that says it believes in sustainable development. What does it do instead? It votes down, in this House, a motion that would have made the Department of Industry, Science and Technology responsible, among other things, for sustainable development.
Obviously, it does not understand the question. How can the government, at this stage, say: "Should Canada commit itself to targets for the emission of carbon dioxide?" How can it even ask that question? How can we have the Minister of Energy out in Vancouver saying: "Should Canada act before the rest of the world acts, or should we wait for everybody else? Should the government seek to establish agreements with the western provinces on emissions?" How can those questions even be asked when we know how urgent and serious this situation is?
This report does not at all address sustainable development. It does not address the problems of the Third World. We know that one of the greatest causes of environmental degradation is poverty. Does this plan talk about what kinds of aid we provide to the Third World, ensuring that that aid is done in an environmentally compatible way, in fact, specifically directing our aid towards projects that assist Third World countries to avoid environmental damage?
Does it talk about the millions of dollars that we provide through the Export Development Corporation to do major projects abroad in China, India, Indonesia and Thailand? Does it put any limits on how we spend that money and make sure that we are not exporting environmentally damaging technology? It does not. In fact, one of the things holding up environmental assessment legislation is that the Export Development Corporation, for the purposes of aiding business clients, is specifically seeking to exempt itself from that legislation.
It does not talk about what we import and whether we encourage pollution in the Third World by importing goods that perhaps we would be better off not importing. It does not talk about how we control our exports to ensure that we are not exporting damaging goods or goods that can be used in a way that is damaging to the environment.
It does not talk about aboriginal rights. A small country like New Zealand can bring in comprehensive environmental legislation which gives prime importance to the rights of aboriginal peoples, their land rights, their treaty rights and their cultural traditions and a country like Canada cannot. It is appalling that that is not even discussed in this paper.
March 30, 1990

The report talks about consultation. The minister who spoke this morning said consultation is desired and needed. Consultation gets off to a bad start when the report on which it is to be based ignores the consultation, ignores the thousands and perhaps millions of words of input this government has received over the years it has been in office from environmental groups. Options which they have developed and put forward are not in this plan. How can they expect the consultation is going to mean anything?
The report said: "Women are a real key to decisionmaking. Aboriginal peoples need to be involved in our discussions. Youth need to be part of our solutions." Just look at what this government has done to those groups. It has diminished the ability of women's groups to participate in society as groups. It has cut funding to women's organizations. It has cut funding for conferences. It has cut funding for women's centres. It is undermining their ability to be informed, to communicate with each other and to communicate with government.
What has it done to aboriginal peoples? A year ago it was cutting its commitment to meet the educational needs of aboriginal peoples and it is still true that a native person in Canada has a much better chance of going to prison than to university. That is a crying indictment of our society. Now it has cut broadcasting, it has cut newspapers, it has cut the means by which natives inform themselves and communicate with each other. It has cut their tools to participate in the democratic process. How dare this paper then say that we want the involvement of aboriginal peoples.
It has cut NGOs' budgets and yet it is saying that they are the crux to our doing something about this problem.
What has it done to youth? Oh, yes, the minister wants youth employment for summer employment programs, he says, summer employment programs on the environment. I am sitting in a riding where summer employment programs this year are one-tenth of what they were last year; $23,000 for a community of 70,000 people for summer employment. How do we expect youth to feel a part of this society when money that could have employed them for the summer and sent them back to school this fall is being pulled out of summer employment for them?
Supply
This is a new kind of consultation. I think the normal process, when there is a discussion paper, is for the parliamentary committee to hold hearings and report back to Parliament. I really want some answers on why that is not being done. Is it that these are going to be secret consultations? Why is the environment committee not being asked to take this document, to consult and to report to Parliament?
I want to close with one final point. Yesterday, the Prime Minister referred to Madam Bruntland's comments about Canada and the leadership role we have played. That was a nice comment from a lead speaker at a conference to the host country. What the Prime Minister failed to say is that Canada essentially holds great conferences, exercises great rhetorical leadership. But what she went on to say was that it was time for Canada to get on with action and demonstrate that its leadership is more than words. This plan is a betrayal of that call to action for Canada and the world.

We know that they want to talk about a new transportation policy. They have just cut VIA Rail, one of the most environmentally friendly systems there is. They just cut VIA Rail.
I want to talk about the green environment we are supposed to be looking towards and The Green Paper we got. The recycling program has not been put by this government to Canadians yet. We have paper recycling projects. And clean water. Well, this is a watered down set of promises.
I want to ask the member, since she has knowledge of government and knowledge as the spokesperson for the environment: Does she not believe, as I do, that it is about time this government put its money where its mouth is and practised environmentally friendly things such as waste management in its own federal government buildings. Should that not be under control?

That is exactly why I put the challenge to all ministers opposite or all those who occasionally speak to them, because I think that is exactly where it has to start. We cannot preach to Canadians what they should be doing in their homes, offices or factories, until we have our own house in order. This is the largest employer in the country. It employs a quarter of a million people directly, and another quarter of a million
people indirectly. We use more paper, more of everything that can be used in an office or laboratory environment than any other employer in Canada. We use more vehicles, we use more energy and, therefore, we should be leading the way.
This also gives me the opportunity to talk about costs. The Minister of Forestry and the Minister of the Environment have said we have got to talk about trade-offs. We have got to talk about costs.
The reason it is so important for the government to act as a leader and as an example is to demonstrate the fact that when things are done in an environmentally sustainable way, money is saved. If factories are built that use fewer resources and less energy, they operate more efficiently and are more productive. Innovative companies that have taken these steps are proving exactly that.
I challenge the government to prove that as a major corporation in this country, the largest corporation, we can demonstrate that it is cheaper and not more expensive to do things the right way. I will challenge that it is going to cost more money. We keep saying that to people and we keep scaring people with it. We keep pretending that we cannot act because it is going to cost too much money.
There are many ways in which it is cheaper. So let us stop pretending.

Mr. Speaker, in her eloquent speech the hon. member identified a very important element in our common efforts to achieve the very worthy environmental goals that we have in Canada.
Specifically that very important element is the relationship between the federal government and the governments of our provinces and territories. The hon. member knows that it is this relationship that is fundamental, not only for success in environmental policy development, but in determining the degree of success in other policy areas.
Would the hon. member share with this House and with Canadians her vision and the vision of her party, with respect to a workable, reasonable and effective framework that would ensure co-operative federal-provincial policy development in the very important area of Canada's environment.
March 30, 1990

Mr. Speaker, obviously I do not have time left to deal with that. However, as the municipal politician who was involved with provincial governments all over the country, I certainly think I have some very valuable ideas to bring not only to a bi-level approach but a tri-level approach to the environment. It was that experience at the local level of government that led me to propose one useful suggestion which I note the minister has adopted for a participaction program on the environment.
To stand aside, do nothing and absolve oneself of any responsibility for the environment is not at all helpful to federal-provincial relationships, or to public confidence in government at all levels. I certainly do not think that the federal government should be dithering around asking silly questions such as whether or not we should reach agreement with the provinces on emissions. Of course we should. Where is the leadership in this country? Who speaks for the nation any more? What are we? Do we just sit here in this House to let the provinces go off and do exactly what they want no matter what the risk to the world, to the helpless Canadians, to the future survival of humanity? Where is the leadership?
You want an answer to your question. Step aside and let me show you.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that most Canadians and probably many citizens throughout the world have concluded that environmental issues should not be partisan issues. They believe that the importance of preserving our future is one which must go beyond the lines of party politics.
I am not so certain, however, that the introductory speech by the hon. member for Hamilton East today furthered the cause of trying to keep environmental issues within this House in as non-partisan a manner as possible.
I believe that most members of the House and most Canadians very much share the common objective of wanting to ensure that the environment upon which we are dependent for our very life itself is conserved and protected. The challenge of finding a means to direct society to the road of an environmentally sustainable future is the most important challenge of our lives. At stake, as Madam Brundtland said, is our common future.
Supply
A challenge is evident. What is less evident, however, is the question of how we should collectively meet that challenge. The behaviour and assumptions which have contributed to the environmental crisis which is very much a part of our life are deeply ingrained in our society's most cherished institutions and values. Consequently, there is no simple change, no single change that will set matters right. What must occur instead is a renaissance of awareness with respect to the restraints that must be respected if our society is to continue to evolve and to progress on an environmentally sustainable path.
A sustainable future is not within the powers of the Minister of the Environment alone, nor is it within the powers of the federal government alone to achieve and to deliver. The scale of the challenge which is before us dwarfs the abilities of any one actor to resolve. All of us, at all levels of government, in all walks of life, wherever we may live in this country and throughout the global community, have a role to play and we are seeking to play that role to the best of our abilities. We, as a government, are committed to doing what is in our power to move Canadians onto a sustainable path.
Yesterday, the Minister of the Environment released a document called "A Framework for Discussion on the Environment". This framework summarizes issues which will be addressed in The Green Plan. It outlines a range of possible solutions which could contribute to the national objective of ensuring the effective integration of economic and environmentally sustainable decision-making, of ensuring that we have sustainable development. Through this document, we hope to engage all Canadians in a national dialogue on our common future.
Throughout the spring, we will be holding consultations with Canadians, in 30 or 40 communities throughout the country, to allow them to express their views on the policies and priorities which should be contained in The Green Plan. It is our hope that through this process of establishing a national dialogue we can achieve the broadest possible consensus on the key elements of this national action plan to ensure a sustainable future for Canada. There will be a full action plan by this fall. It will be substantial, meaningful, and will build on the solid record of achievement of this government. In addition, it will be constructed as a result of a process of consulta-

March 30, 1990
Supply
tion with Canadians, the likes of which has not occurred before in this country.
In this national green plan we will seek creative partnerships with the provinces, with interest groups and with industries. We are willing to consider participation in any arrangement which will set an example to others or which will promote collective progress. We will continue to work internationally through whatever means that are available to us whether it be the G-7, the United Nations, the Commonwealth, the Francophonie, NATO, the World Bank, or in co-operation with the Inter-American Development Bank to whom the Minister of the Environment is speaking today. We will do all of this in order to promote the need for environmen-tally-sustainable development.
Our environmental destiny here in Canada is tied to the global environmental destiny. We must recognize the essentiality of that fact. All Canadians must adopt the principle of thinking globally while acting locally. In a global sense, Canada has not only been an active participant on the international scene but has been a leader in that international environmental arena. Canada's leading role in the development of the 1987 Montreal Protocol on protecting the ozone layer is well known to all parliamentarians and to most Canadians.
In the following year, Canada hosted an international conference on "The Changing Atmosphere, Implications for Global Security". While addressing that conference, the Prime Minister was the first to call for an international convention to protect the atmosphere to be held by 1992. The concept of the need for that convention is now supported by President Bush, Prime Minister Thatcher, President Mitterand and many other national leaders.
Last March the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Environment represented Canada at the Environmental Summit at The Hague, where world leaders agreed to develop within the United Nations an enhanced authority to combat global warming. Also in March of last year, this government was one of 34 signatories to a landmark United Nations convention, which controls the transboundary movement of hazardous waste.
Last July in Paris, Canada joined other economic leaders in placing the environment at the top of the international agenda.
In Kuala Lumpur, in October, leaders of all 49 Commonwealth nations endorsed the concept of sustainable development.
Looking ahead to 1992, the world will gather for what is probably going to be the most important environmental conference held since the landmark Stockholm conference of 1972. That conference will be the United Nations Conference on the Environment and Development which will be held in Brazil and of which a distinguished Canadian, Maurice Strong, will be the chairman.
It is expected that world leaders will meet at this conference to conclude a landmark convention on climate change, if indeed that convention is not concurred with prior to the meetings in 1992. Scientific and legal work for this convention has been under way for some time and good progress is being made.
We want Canada to set an example for the world, but we must be realistic and recognize that our efforts alone cannot achieve worldwide change. We must work co-operatively with other countries and also through all international organizations that can mobilize actions on a global scale. We recognize the need as well to work co-operatively to protect the environment of the North American continent. One example of such co-operation between Canada and the United States is the establishment of the North America Waterfowl Management Plan, a plan which provides for $1.5 billion over 15 years to protect almost 4 million acres of wetland habitat in Canada.
Canada is also working closely with the United States to clean up the Great Lakes. Our share of that program is $125 million to be spent over the next five years to protect human health, to clean up toxic contamination and to prevent future pollution of these important shared resources.
I am encouraged by recent news stories coming out of the United States with respect to the progress which the American Congress is making towards the passage of President Bush's Clean Air Bill. This government has worked closely with our counterparts in the United States, encouraging them to pass that bill. I hope that
March 30, 1990

that will not only be a reality in the near future but it will be followed as well by an accord between our two countries.
Closer to home, despite what you may have heard earlier today, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that this government has a solid record of achievement on which to build.
In June, 1988 the Canadian Environmental Protection Act was proclaimed, the strongest piece of environmental legislation ever sponsored by a federal government in Canada. CEPA, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, establishes very stringent controls for chemical substances manufactured in or imported into Canada and provides for a "cradle to grave" mechanism for managing such substances from their manufacture to their disposal.
In addition, the federal and provincial governments are working co-operatively on a number of environmental issues through the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment. That group met last week at Globe 90 in Vancouver. Last October, the council established the creation of a $250 million fund based upon a 50-50 federal-provincial cost sharing formula to clean up high risk abandoned contaminated land sites, the sites that we refer to as orphan sites.
At the same time, the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment announced a joint decision to implement standards to control automobile emissions of oxides of nitrogen and gasoline fumes, which will match, by 1994, the toughest standards in North America. We generally refer to those standards as the California standards.
Another example of federal-provincial co-operation which is noteworthy is the agreement to clean up the St. Lawrence River. In June, 1988 this federal government announced a $110 million action plan to tackle industrial pollution in this major waterway.
Throughout Canada and the world, national parks have proved to be one of the most effective ways of protecting wilderness, wildlife and other important heritage resources. Since 1984, this government has added greatly to that national park system. Three new national parks and park reserves have been established: Ellesmere on Canada's most northerly lands; Bruce Peninsula near the heart-of Ontario and within easy reach of
Supply
millions of Canadians; and South Moresby on the spectacular Queen Charlotte Islands.
In addition, park establishment agreements for two other areas were renegotiated so that the parks could realize their full potential, helping to consolidate the system: Grasslands, protecting a remnant of the wild prairie ecosystem in the western part of Saskatchewan; and Pacific Rim, preserving an unspoiled example of the west coast on Vancouver Island.
In addition, a policy for establishing, developing and operating national marine parks has been approved, and Canada's first national marine park, Fathom Five, was established in Georgian Bay, Ontario. One of the most important aspects of the document which was tabled by the minister yesterday was the commitment that five additional national parks should be created during the course of the next five years.
I would hope in passing, Mr. Speaker, although it is too early to tell, that one of those additional parks might indeed be in my own home province of Manitoba near the community of Churchill.
Much remains to be done and this government is committed to doing it. For example, the federal government will be introducing shortly a regulatory package that will limit pollution from pulp and paper mills. These new regulations will achieve the virtual elimination of dioxin and furan discharges in mill effluents.
If there is a special role for the federal government in environmental protection, I would suggest it is the development of national standards and practices. This is clear from our current efforts to reform the federal Environmental Assessment Review Process, or what we commonly refer to as EARP.
The objective of EARP is to enable the government to encourage environmentally appropriate development. That objective, however, cannot be achieved if the process is flawed and unclear, as has now been demonstrated to be the case. New EARP legislation, as I indicated earlier in the House today, will be introduced this spring. I know that members of the House will look forward to supporting that legislation because they understand that there is a very real need for clarity and certainty in the vital matter of assessing the environmental implications of government decisions especially on major projects.

Environmental stewardship is not only an individual effort. Partners, by working together, can achieve great results. I think, for example, of the $50 million Environmental Partners Fund whose goal is to tap the creative talents of Canadians and establish community-oriented environmental projects, with up to half of that fund being provided by the federal government. Some $3.6 million has already been approved for 76 projects across Canada, and I am delighted that one of them is my own constituency of Brandon-Souris which is enabling members of the Virden community to expand the recycling project that they have had in place for some time.
Yesterday, the Minister of the Environment released a framework for discussion on the environment. We are inviting all Canadians to participate in the challenge of developing a long-term action plan for Canada's environment. The goal is to translate the concept of the sustainable development into a concrete reality. The Green Plan must be based upon a comprehensive policy which will be taking tough decisions on sensitive issues. The Green Plan will provide a decision-making framework for planning so we can anticipate and prevent problems before they occur. It will alter the federal government's own day-to-day environmental behaviour.
The Green Plan is based on the knowledge that balancing economic and environmental concerns will without a doubt be the greatest challenge of our time. Moreover, if sustainable development is going to work, then all sectors of society, governments, business and individuals must work together.
The achievement of an environmentally sustainable economic development will require change by all Canadians, acting individually or collectively within governments or the business community. It will require new attitudes towards the environment and its relationship to our own day-to-day activities. It will demand a commitment to take action.
The Green Plan for Canada will provide the basis for that change. It will enable Canadians to make wiser decisions about the use of the environment through better science and technology, better information and education and tougher regulations.
The Green Plan will be developed as a result of a process of consulting together. All sectors of Canada are invited to be a part of that process. We will achieve a broad consensus on what should be done and we will have the support of Canadians when we bring that plan into this House in the fall.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member. Seeing the paper that the government came out with concerning the environment, the protection of the environment, and toxic waste, I am not going to try and pretend that I have a great knowledge of the different kinds of systems we need for the environment. When I was in the Quebec National Assembly, I lived through many problems of the environment that arose, such as toxic wastes that created a crisis that used to last for weeks and then subside.
It seems that it is only the government which can have the political will and the power to show to all Canadians that the environment is our number one issue. The paper that came out seems to be very vague. It seems to me that the federal government, of all the governments in this country, should be the first to have the most stringent rules of all and there should be nothing vague. The message should go out to all industries as clear as a bell that protecting the environment 100 per cent is the cost of doing business in this country. That might sound idealistic, but because of the way the environment is being affected, we are going to face that inevitability very soon.
Why can the federal government not take it upon itself to send the message out across this country that we want an environmental policy that is virtually foolproof?

speechtext:

complaining. In the meantime, what we have developed in the framework announced yesterday is a process by which we hope to achieve that end. We hope to work with both levels of government because the natural resources are a part of the prerogative of the provinces, according to the constitution.
They have responsibility themselves for protecting the environment. The classic example is the debate which is occurring right now between the federal government and the province of Quebec with respect to our desires that James Bay be assessed according to federal regulations as well as provincial regulations. The two levels of government need to work together in co-operation with business and with interested groups, but the final result must be that clear signal so that we all understand what our responsibilities are and where the powers are very clear. I truly believe that that will be the end result.
In the meantime, I would ask the hon. member to be a part of the process of developing that end result. I think that is what this framework is asking of Canadians. It is providing them with an opportunity to be a part of the solution. All governments have been guilty, but what has happened too often in this country is a government or perhaps bureaucrats who have tried to lay a solution on to other people, perhaps without their understanding of what is required and often without their co-operation.
The environment is something which is of vital importance to all of us. Surely we all understand that and surely there will be a willingness to work together towards a common solution, if we can achieve a broad national consensus on what needs to be done. I would readily concede that many environmental groups have led the way in demonstrating the need. Governments are often slow to respond. I would suggest that previous federal governments have been slow to respond, and some provincial governments are slow to respond.
I think the most important question is, what is on the table when we are finished? If we work together in this House and throughout the country and participate in the consultation process, I honestly believe we will have The Green Plan in place in the fall in which we can all share some sense of pride in being a part of what I hope will be a good solution.

Mr. Speaker, if we are to have a good consultative process, it is important not to put out vague questions, which the plan does, but clear alternatives for action within some analysis of the pros and cons. Then communities, business and whoever else is a stakeholder in the situation has something to respond to. Clearly, the paper does not do that, even though those possible solutions are well known. I would like the parliamentary secretary to answer two questions. First, the consultative process is extremely unclear. We start with a series of information sessions. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The hon. member for Windsor-St. Clair.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague for Chambly earlier said that the minister was a good and sincere man, a minister of the environment who finds himself in a very bad environment.
It seems to me it is clear that we are faced with this almost ridiculous situation by virtue of the fact that those on the government side who should have provided him with the support in putting forth the kind of environmental strategy that we expected did not give him that support. We are left with a document that we could be trite about and say that it is fatally flawed, but in fact its structure is not substantial enough even to exhibit flaws. It is incomplete. It has not hardly begun the process of a strategy. As a matter of fact, considering all of the resources that are available to a government, all of the resources that ought to have been provided to this minister, given the urgency of what is at issue here, the document The Green Plan for Canada, a federal agenda prepared by voluntary organizations, would have been a far superior document to present to the Canadian people even within this context of consultation because at least they would have had some meat with which to deal as they have not here.
Many have cited the fact that a lot of questions have been posed for which answers have already, at least in large measure, been provided. But there are some questions so ludicrous that no one in his right mind would have asked them in the first place.
Let me give you an example. I want you to pay attention to this, Mr. Speaker, because there are no subtleties in this that would make it sensible to ask this question: Should Canada commit itself to greenhouse gas emission targets? Should we or should we not? Should we allow the earth to warm up over the next two or three decades? Do we want those dramatic changes in weather and climate that have been predicted by all of those who have been engaged in the study of the earth's
March 30, 1990

atmosphere? I do not think there is a single Canadian who would not say that this is a silly question.
Then there is the question: What role should alternative energy and energy efficiency play? Give me a break. This is a question posed by a minister who is supposed to be in charge of Canada's environmental policy. Should there be alternative energy? I suppose that there is only one basis for the government asking this question. Having already closed down research on alternative energy, the government is now scratching its head and saying, "should we have done that?". Of course this is one of those questions the answer to which has already been provided. The people have said that there should be a commitment to alternative energy and efficiency and the government has said, no there should not be. We have the Minister of the Environment hastening back, puzzled altogether, not knowing what to do, the two sides having different responses so he is going to pose the question again.
I can tell him right now that there should be an emphasis on alternative energy and there should be greater investment in energy efficiency. My goodness, it is not more than a year and a half ago that all sides of this House approved a motion to have a hydrogen technology project in this country. That is one example of alternative energy, the research into which has been cut by this government.
To give you another example of the absurd, Mr. Speaker, is the proposal that additional assistance should be given to developing countries to adopt sustainable forestry practices. I do not know whether the Minister of Forestry is here. He was a little while ago, but I guess he could not stand the heat. Now we are going to help the Third World nations do something to enhance sustainable forestry and we have a question in this document that is as follows: How should Canada move towards sustainable forest management? It certainly cannot be by allowing forestry agreements to lapse tomorrow. This document holds not only itself up to ridicule, but the government which authored it, and it is an insult to Canadians.
My colleague next to me says that the Government of Canada must lead by example. This gives me an opportunity to draw to your attention a situation in which the government has not provided a very good example.

This is an example that comes out of southwestern Ontario, in Windsor, where the government has not provided a very good example in the way it has confronted the issue of the incinerator in Detroit which still, after four years, is a problem which has not been confronted by our government. I note that the document talks about the need for negotiating a trans-boundary air pollution agreement with the United States. I am glad to hear the government is finally getting the message. We have been asking for that for four years. It is the only tenable way of attacking that issue.
We have the issue of the FERMI nuclear plant, and we have been trying to get the government to negotiate some kind of general agreement in recognition of the fact that this government has apparently just learned that pollution and environmental damage knows no national boundaries. But not much has been happening there either.
We have been trying to get the Minister of Transport to address the fact that barges will be going back and forth between Detroit and Windsor, carrying railway cars with hazardous substances. But he does not know anything about that. He does not know what he is supposed to do about that, nor does he know who is supposed to do anything about that. This is government by example.
I want to tie this business of government by example in with its proposition that innovative science and technology must be supported. I would just like to say in passing that one of the things that this document suggests is to put some emphasis on research into the environment, into the programs of the granting councils which provide funding for basic research in the universities.
The government has already ignored recommendations for vastly enhanced investment in that. Now, I suppose it is going to cut that by half, turn that over to environmental research with no net increase in research, and announce that it has put that $200 million into environmental research whenever it gets around to it. That is the kind of example, that is the kind of innovative science and technology we have.
In 1981 Environment Canada reported the dangers and risks involved in a contamination of the Great Lakes by biota from European waters. It was noted that if one looked in the ballasts of ships coursing the Atlantic Ocean, they were a virtual zoo of aquatic animals which might adapt to the Great Lakes environment, but constitute a severe disturbance to the ecological balance. That is the ecosystem which is the Great Lakes. They warned

particularly of the zebra mussel. They said that there ought to be imposed strict regulations on the emptying of ballast tanks from sea-going vessels from Europe into the Great Lakes. That was in 1981.
By 1986 those mussels were found. In the meantime, in 1985, at the behest of this government the scientists who made the recommendation were let go. The first of these mussels was detected in 1986. In 1988 there were indications that there was going to be a problem. Now, when each of these little critters produces 40,000 eggs a piece, it is possible to find in areas of the Great Lakes and in some areas at the bottom 700,000 of these sharp shelled, ugly, sticky little critters. Now they are fouling the water intakes of towns such as Leamington, Sarnia and so on.
In Leamington they are spending a million dollars in order to make it possible to bring water into the water supply system so great is the fouling of the intakes by these precocious multipliers. Their numbers will double again by next year.
It is not just a matter of the inconvenience of fouling the water intakes. They affected Lake St. Clair first because apparently the emptying of the ballast occurred in the neighbourhood of Sarnia, just previous to a deliveiy to Sarnia. Now they are found in Lake Erie and Lake St. Clair.
One of the things one notices as a result of the infestation of these lakes is that the lakes have become more clear. They have become clear because these critters eat algae in copious quantities. The food of commercial fish in Lake Erie is being consumed by these foreigners and it is likely that the economic value of the fisheries in Lake Erie will be halved as a consequence of the invasion of these mussels.
I do not want to give the impression that the emptying of ballast tanks in the Great Lakes has only led to zebra mussels. That is a serious enough problem. But there is also a little perch-like fish that will replace the perch, a fish of commercial value, in Lake Erie. Again they were introduced by the emptying of ballast tanks. What has been the response of the government that governs by example? There has been a refusal to impose any
regulations or voluntary guidelines that we are told are 85 per cent effective.
Ninety-nine per cent adherence to those voluntary guidelines could still lead to the introduction of one critter into the Great Lakes of similar damaging characteristics and that would be all that is necessary. It must be clear to you as it is clear to any sensible person that there must be something more than guidelines. There must be stiff regulations to ensure that no other foreign critters can be introduced to the Great Lakes which will destroy the Great Lakes ecosystem.
In addition to this being the example of government by example, you should note that it is the IJC's role to ensure the quality of the Great Lakes. Of course we know, as many environmental groups have pointed out, our government has failed, as has the American government, to do its job.
The Americans are not standing still. Senator Glenn has introduced legislation to provide $40 million in research to help those municipalities that have to pick up the costs of the changes in the water intake systems which are going to be imposed upon them by government failure.
There should also be an intensive research program on Canada's part, jointly with the United States, to deal with this problem. We will never rid the lakes of zebra mussels but we can do some things to decrease and control their population.
Diving ducks such as the canvas back and others feed on these things. It may be that controls on the hunting of these birds would be helpful. There may be other techniques.
The point is that we have not got time for questions and answers or any similar games that the government imposes on the minister rather than action. We want action whether we are municipal taxpayers or commercial fishermen in the Great Lakes. We want action if it be only because we love the Great Lakes and the ecosystem in its balance, which presents so much beauty to us.
We do not want a government which, by example, does nothing. We do not want a government that talks about the necessary research to address the problem instead of

doing something about the problem. I have set out only example of the failure of this government and of the previous government. The people are getting tired of it.
In Windsor, where there is a particular environmental consciousness, we are sick to death of questions. We want answers.

Mr. Speaker, before I commence my remarks on this extremely important motion, I would just like to pay a compliment to our newest colleague in the House on his maiden speech, the hon. member for Chambly, although I warn him his last remarks were so long that I almost changed my mind about the compliment. However, I do offer it in good faith and good spirit.
This is a crucially important motion. It is a crucially important matter. This is possibly the most important matter facing Parliament and the people of Canada today as we enter into the last decade of the 20th century.
As most people know, I represent the city of Halifax in the Province of Nova Scotia. The Province of Nova Scotia is known and acknowledged far and wide across this country as one of the most beautiful places, not just

in this beautiful country of Canada, but one of the most beautiful places on earth.
Our licence plates proclaim us as "Canada's Ocean Playground". We are almost an island. We are connected to the rest of Canada by the isthmus of Chignecto, a scant 12 miles wide, and we are surrounded almost completely by the waters of the Atlantic Ocean, the Bay of Fundy and the Northumberland Strait. We have within our province the beautiful Bradore Lakes, a number of rivers that once, and I say sadly, were teaming with Atlantic salmon, and the wonderful chains of lakes that make up part and parcel of the Kedgemakooge National Park in the southern part of our province.
When Europeans first came to the shores of Nova Scotia in the year 1603, they knew what a beautiful and magnificent country they had settled in. When the first Europeans, the French, came to Nova Scotia, followed soon after by Scots, Irish, English, Germans and many other nations, they settled in this province and they farmed, fished and did some logging.
In the northern part of the province they began the coal mines that go three, four, five and six miles out under the sea, and the steelworks. Even in those early days when they began the steelworks and the coal mines, they were concerned about the environmental reaction, about the way the land, the sky and the water would react to the industrial development in that most beautiful of provinces, Nova Scotia.
To a degree, we do not have so much to worry about from our own home-grown industry any more because the coal industry is almost dead and the steel industry in danger of dying. The beauties of Nova Scotia are imperilled on a daily basis and the change over the last few years has been frightening to those of us who live within this province.
My family has a house 30 miles outside the city of Halifax on the shores of St. Margaret's Bay, very close to one of the most famous landmarks in Nova Scotia, and I refer to Peggy's Cove. Those of you who have not been there, I invite you to come. But I invite you to come fairly quickly while its beauty is still evident to all.
I tell you that on the shores of St. Margaret's Bay, for years people from Halifax and the surrounding area and tourists who come to our province, have used the beaches, gone swimming, sailing, fishing and all the various recreational activities that can be done in Cana-

da's Ocean Playground. Those days are dying because of what is happening to those waters.
Last summer, on one of the few days when I had a chance to spend some time at this house, I came out early in the morning to look at the harbour in front of my house and I saw, washing up with the tide, milk cartons, garbage and the detritus of every day life in our overpackaged, garbage-choked society.
Our hon. colleague from Windsor-St. Clair talk about the ad with the aboriginal North American with the tear running down his face because of the damage to the environment. That is a very moving advertisement, I agree.
The one I was reminded of is one that is equally familiar to many Canadians. That was one for which a former CBC broadcaster, Stanley Burke, did the voice over. You saw the earth, garbage being poured on the earth, garbage being thrown at the earth, and I think the final visual was a cigar butt being put out on the side of the globe. I remember that ad from when I was a university student which, in spite of my youthful appearance, was not yesterday.
The knowledge that the protection of the environment has to be and must be the A-l priority for government's world-wide is not new. It is not something that was bom in the minds of politicians and governments yesterday. It certainly is not something born in the minds of only Canadians, but of people world-wide.
The environmental movement has been a moving force on our earth for many years. In the last couple of years many involved in the environmental movement began to feel a greater sense of accomplishment, purpose and enthusiasm because suddenly we realized that politicians, elected officials and governments recognized the fact that environmental questions were of major concern.
The framework of the government's discussion on the environment is a blow to the sense of light, purpose, accomplishment and hope. We do not need a framework for discussion. That is fine. It is all very well and good. It is printed on recycled paper, which we applaud. But, what we need is action. We do not need to discuss any longer. We know what the problems are. We know what
we have to do. We know what is necessary to stop poisoning our lakes, rivers and oceans.
We know what is necessary to end acid rain. We know what is necessary to stop oil spills. We have the answers. Environmentalists have told us time and again that we also have the technology. What the framework for discussion on the environment manifests to all Canadians today is the lack of political will.
I see my colleague and my friend from Cumberland- Colchester has come into the House. I know he would agree with me because just two weeks ago I drove through his beautiful riding of Cumberland-Colchester with the wonderful rolling hills and waterways and the beautiful Bay of Fundy. But, the garbage is rolling up on the beaches in Cumberland county, just as it is rolling up on the beaches of Halifax county, just as it is rolling up on the beautiful beaches within the riding of the member for South Shore, the member for Halifax West and the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants.
The Conservative members from the province of Nova Scotia know what pollution, over-packaging, acid rain and oil spills are doing to what was once a pristine environment in the province of Nova Scotia. We were given this land to nurture us and to nurture our children. What we are doing by refusing to create the political will that will preserve this land is committing long-term suicide for ourselves and for future generations. When the planet is laid waste, if we do not take action now, today in 1990, there will be no one else to blame but the men and women who sat in the House today and proceeded to do nothing more than discuss.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to follow my colleague, an outstanding spokesperson from the maritimes, who has expressed herself most eloquently on this question. I would like to know from her what kind of readjustment schedules will be necessary in her region as it move towards more sustainable growth in developing alternate uses of fuel, alternate methods of local and indigenous economic development.
How can it be possible when the government is cutting back on regional programs? How can it be possible and what kind of problems are going to be faced when this paper asks you to meet this challenge with talk, talk, talk and no action. I would like to hear from you, Madam Member, through the Chair, exactly how you are going

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. I realize that in his own experience as a provincial premier he knows the difficulties in dealing with federal governments. One of the things I mentioned in my speech is that the former industrial strategies in the province of Nova Scotia had perhaps less than full environmental approval. I am referring of course to both the steel plants and the coal mines. That, as I said, is no longer a problem.
The ideas of alternate energy sources in Nova Scotia at the moment include coal. As the hon. member is aware, there are several coal mines running in the province. Unfortunately, they are running at a loss. The products from these coal mines are firing a number of electrical generating plants in the province of Nova Scotia, but sadly these plants have to be subsidized because there is no real plan for alternate fuel other than fossil fuel. There is no real commitment from either the provincial government in the province of Nova Scotia or from the federal government to assist hard-pressed, economically depressed provinces like Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland.
These are some of the most beautiful places on earth and we are throwing them away because there is no political will and there is no plan. Those before such as Nova Scotia's Ecology Action Centre have long and noble service in giving advice to government, which is virtually ignored. As the hon. member for Esquimalt- Juan de Fuca was saying, those people are ignored both by provincial governments and certainly by this federal government. We have various environmental strategies but nothing but deaf ears do they fall on, here with the Mulroney government and back home with the Buchanan government.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to compliment my hon. colleague for a most important discourse on this important subject of the environment. It also taught me a few new things about another part of the country with which I was not that familiar. But I would like to ask my hon. colleague a question dealing with how Canadians see the role of government which was touched upon throughout The

Green Paper. I would like to begin my question by referring to a poll that was taken two years ago. They discovered that, if a company repeatedly pollutes at unsafe levels, over nine out of ten Canadians want corporate executives held personally and I emphasize that, personally responsible. Sixty three per cent favour fines but a whopping 19 per cent of Canadians say corporate executives should be jailed. I would like to ask my hon. colleague if she agrees with the assessment of two out of ten Canadians that corporate polluters who flout the regulations on a federal level or on a provincial level should go to jail?

Mr. Speaker, I think the responsibility of board members of corporations should be more serious than merely a financial burden. With jail sentences we get into jurisdictional problems vis-a-vis criminal law and civil law. Should there be criminal sanctions for environmental infractions? I think the answer is most definitely yes. Whether it should be jail or not, I think would depend on the infraction and what happened exactly.
I think we should have a section of the Criminal Code relating to environmental crime. I think sanctions should not merely be in the form of fines against a corporation but the people who run the corporation should be held liable personally. I am not prepared to go as far as jail. We will have to see the individual situation.
Mr. Speaker, I find myself a little puzzled by the contradiction that appears here. Perhaps the hon. member can help me out.
With pleasure.

I am sure it will be. On issues such as the GST, VTA Rail and government cut-backs, the opposition insists on consultation with the people. It wants hearings across Canada. It wants the public to have its say.
The Green Plan does exactly that. It gives the people in my riding an opportunity to have a say in what can be done to address environmental problems in our area. There are 35 meetings scheduled and more may be added. I find it a contradiction that the GST is important enough to let people voice their opinions as is VIA Rail

Some areas in my riding experience 40 per cent unemployment. If the government were to impose environmental regulations without consultation, there could be detrimental effects which hurt a lot of people.

Mr. Speaker, first, in answer to the member for Cumberland-Colchester, the people of Canada have been telling governments for 20 years their opinions on the environment. Unfortunately, the people of Canada did not have an opportunity to tell the government their opinions on the GST because it was sprung on them a scant two years ago in embryo.
With regard to the environment not being important enough, that is not worthy of the member for Cumberland-Colchester. He knows we all feel the environment is important. I do not deny that. What I deny is the way they go about working it through.
This is similar to a suggestion that we hold more hearings on child care. Clean out your ears, gentlemen. The people of Canada have told you, and told you, and told you, what they want the government to do about child care. They have told you, and told you, and told you, what they want the government to do about the environment. They want it cleaned up. They want it cleaned up now, and they want it clean for their kids. They do not want a 7 per cent goods and services tax, but you brought that up, I did not.

I would also like to say that on The Green Plan the government says it wants to consult with the aboriginal people. It is good that it finally wants to do that. However, we have been waiting for that for years. We have been waiting for somebody to ask us what we think of the environment because we are intimately involved with the environment. They should have been asking us when they were debating the Oldman River Dam, the Rafferty-Alameda, James Bay and the proposed pulp mills in Alberta. We have just been waiting to be asked.
Another issue that I would like to touch on is the issue of the Inuit people and the environment. Some years ago, a French movie star started the whole thing. Brigitte Bardot, with the help of Greenpeace, destroyed a livelihood that the Newfoundland people had as well as the Inuit people in the north, without asking us, without asking us what we thought about whether there should be seal hunts in Newfoundland, never realizing that it was going to destroy two livelihoods-the Inuit and the Newfoundland people.
Again we could have given them some advice on how to go about dealing with the environment, but they did not choose to do that. Now, in retrospect, they say: "Well, we did not mean to destroy the Inuit way of life''. Generous, very generous after the fact. So what do we say to people like the environmentalists? We have no problems with the environmentalists as long as we can work with them and the government is willing to listen to us. But to people like Greenpeace and others, what we would say to them is: "Don't call us we will call you".
Now the same thing is happening with the anti-fur movement. What really bothers me is that these people think they know best, either environmentalists or antifur movement, animal rights people. All these guys are saying is: "We do not want you to hunt; we do not want you to trap". The animal rights group think, I am sure, that steaks come from the supermarket. I mean that is how they think, that chickens come from the supermarket, that they do not need to be killed or plucked or skinned, and all that. It boggles the mind as to how insensitive, for lack of a better word, these people can be.
In terms of the anti-fur and animal rights group, what they do not realize is that we do not contribute to the

damage to the environment. In getting the fur or the seal skin there is very little damage if any to the environment. However, I should say that those people who are animal rights groups should think about what they are wearing in terms of manufacturing, what it did to the environment in manufacturing their jacket, their shirt, whatever, their rayon, nylon, whatever. I think they should be thinking more along that line.
I would just like to touch on the contamination of food. In the north, which I have mentioned previously, the people of Broughton Island, a small community of about 450, are concerned about PCBs and other chemicals in their food chain. They have absolutely nothing to do with the contamination of that food chain. This food chain was through the polar bear or other animals. They got contaminated from the fall down of chemicals that do not know any international boundaries. PCBs do not know that they are not supposed to fall in Canada. They are not supposed to, but they do not know that. Meanwhile, more contamination is happening because there are not enough environmental programs being instituted in various governments, whether it is the federal government or other governments.
I would like to touch on the tanker traffic proposals in the north. When they are talking about the environment in the north, people have to realize it is a very fragile ecological system. We call it Nunatsiaq, the good land. However, Mr. Speaker, if I were to describe Nunatsiaq to you, I would say the beautiful land. I say the good land because it gives us life. That is the difference in how we see the land. We use it and call it the good land.
It is always an honour to address the people here about various issues. I am glad that I had this opportunity to say a few things about the environment.

Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague from Nunatsiaq on his remarks. In particular, I want to raise the fact that last summer, when our colleague hosted our caucus in his riding on Baffin Island, we were told about some other environmental dangers up there such as the dumping of leftover machinery belonging to American military personnel. I am wondering if he would like to make any comments about that this afternoon.

I must admit that I am not sure which minister made a statement about those abandoned Distant Early Warning sites, but the minister said that they would be cleaned up. I do not want to give credit to the wrong minister. I would like to carry on a little further concerning the issue of how environmentally cautious we are in the north. The Inuit Circumpolar Conference, which is the international arm of the Inuit, received a Global 500 Award from the United Nations Environmental Program for: "Outstanding achievements, protection and improvement of the environment".
The work of the Inuit Circumpolar Conference was cited as an example of the world conservation strategy in action. I would hope that measures are taken to clean up the sites that my hon. colleague mentioned, and that
they will be taken soon. This will give us our beautiful land back to its natural state, once it has been used as a Distant Early Warning site or by any other group.
